## Methods

Biological resources
E. coli strain BW25113 was obtained from National BioResource Project E. coli (NBRP-E. coli) at the National Institute of Genetics (Mishima, Japan). The ΔmnmA strain was obtained from the E. coli KEIO collection resource (Tokyo, Japan)76. S. cerevisiae BY4742 (WT) strain (Matα; his3-1; leu2-0; ura3-0) and ctu1Δ strain (BY4742 background) were obtained from EUROSCARF (Germany). Mouse and pig livers were purchased from Funakoshi (Tokyo, Japan). MKN45 (RCB1001), HeLa (RCB0007), HEK293T (RCB2202) and HuH-7 (RCB1366) were obtained from RIKEN BRC (Tsukuba, Japan). A549 (CCL-185), Hep G2 (HB-8065), MCF7 (HTB-22), T24 (HTB-4), and RAW264.7 (TIB-71) were obtained from ATCC. MOLM-13 (C0003003) was obtained from Addexbio (San Diego).

Cell culture
E. coli cells were cultivated in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium with vigorous shaking at 37°C. S. cerevisiae cells were cultivated in Yeast Peptone Dextrose (YPD) medium (2% peptone, 1% yeast extract, and 2% glucose) at 30°C. HeLa, HuH-7, hep G2, MCF7, and A549 cells were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (high-glucose; Sigma) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Corporation). MOLM-13, MKN45, and RAW264.7 cells were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium (Nacalai Tesque) supplemented with 10% FBS. T24 cells were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in McCoy’s 5A (modified) Medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS.

For oxidative stress conditions, HeLa cells were cultured until they reached 70–80% confluency, then treated for 1 h with oxidative stress-inducing agents: 2 mM H2O2 (Nacalai Tesque), 20 μM menadione (Sigma-Aldrich), or 0.25–1 mM rotenone (Tokyo Chemical Industry). Although 2 mM H2O2 is far above the IC50 value for HeLa cells (50 μM), we did not observe any cell detachment nor apoptosis in our condition. Following treatment, cells were washed with PBS. Total RNA was extracted as shown below.

RNA extraction and isolation of individual tRNAs
Total RNA was extracted from E. coli as described77. Briefly, E. coli cells were suspended in a 1:1 mixture of water-saturated phenol and RNA extraction buffer A [50 mM NaOAc (pH 5.2) and 10 mM Mg(OAc)2], followed by two cycles of freeze-thawing with liquid nitrogen, and vigorous stirring for 1 h at room temperature. After centrifugation, the aqueous phase was subjected to chloroform extraction and 2-propanol precipitation.

Total RNA from yeast cells were prepared as follows. Yeast cells were resuspended in 5–10 weights of RNA extraction buffer B [50 mM NaOAc (pH 5.2), 10 mM EDTA, 1% SDS, and 14.3 mM β-mercaptoethanol], and an equal volume of water-saturated phenol was added. The mixture was shaken for 1 h, followed by centrifugation at 8000 × g for 30 min at 4°C. The supernatants were collected, treated with an equal volume of chloroform, followed by isopropanol precipitation. The pellets were dissolved in water, and added with 2% (v/v) 1 M MES-NaOH (pH 6.0), 2.5% (v/v) 5 M NaCl, and 40% (v/v) 2-butoxyethanol. The mixture was then placed on ice for 30 min, followed by centrifugation at 8000 × g for 30 min at 4°C to remove precipitates. The supernatants were subjected to ethanol precipitation to obtain the total RNA. To obtain small RNA fraction, total RNA was subjected to an anion-exchange resin (DEAE Sepharose Fast Flow; Cytiva) in low salt buffer A [20 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 250 mM NaCl, and 2 mM dithiothreitol (DTT)]. After washing the resin with the same buffer, small RNA fractions were eluted with high salt buffer A [20 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 1 M NaCl, and 2 mM DTT].

Total RNA from cultured cells or frozen tissue were prepared using an isolation reagent comprising 40% (w/v) phenol, 1% (v/v) ethyleneglycol, 2 M guanidine thiocyanate, 20 mM tri-sodium citrate, 0.1 M NaOAc (pH 4.5), 0.2% (w/v) N-lauroylsarcosine sodium salt, 50 mM salicylic acid, 10 μM aluminon, 6.9 mM 8-hydroxyquinoline, 0.0001 w/v% BPB. For highly reducing conditions, the same isolation reagent was used with the addition of 50 mM DTT. Alternatively, total RNA were extracted from cultured cells or frozen tissue using TriPure Isolation Reagent (Roche). Frozen tissues were cryogenically ground in a GRINDOMIX GM200 knife mill (Roche) prior to extraction. For further purification, total RNA were subjected to an anion-exchange resin (DEAE Sepharose Fast Flow; Cytiva) in low salt buffer B [10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 250 mM NaCl, and 2 mM DTT], and small RNA fractions were eluted with high salt buffer B [10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 1 M NaCl and 2 mM DTT]. To obtain total tRNA fractions or class I tRNA fractions, total RNA was separated by on 7 M urea denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) and stained with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen), then purified by excising the corresponding gel bands.

Individual tRNAs were isolated by RCC60,78. Sequences of 5′-terminal ethylcarbamate (EC) amino-modified DNA probes (Sigma Aldrich) complementary to target tRNAs are listed in Supplementary Data 6. Each probe was covalently immobilized on NHS-activated Sepharose 4 Fast Flow resin (Cytiva), packed in a custom-made tip, and attached to a custom-made multichannel head on the RCC device. Small RNA fractions obtained by DEAE chromatography were dissolved in 6 × NHE buffer [1.2 M NaCl, 30 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 15 mM EDTA-NaOH pH 8.0 and 1 mM DTT], and passed through the tip by auto-pipetting at 65°C. After washing the tip columns with 0.1 × NHE at 40°C, bound tRNAs were eluted with 0.1 × NHE at 68°C. The purity of isolated tRNAs was confirmed by 10% PAGE with 7 M urea.

RNA mass spectrometry
Isolated tRNAs were digested with RNase T1 and analyzed by capillary LC/nano-ESI-MS as described78–80. One picomole of isolated tRNA was digested with 20 U of RNase T1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 20 mM NH4OAc (pH 5.3) at 37°C for 45 min. A linear ion trap-orbitrap hybrid MS instrument (LTQ Orbitrap XL; Thermo Fisher Scientific) was equipped with a splitless nano HPLC system (DiNa; Techno Alpha) using a nano-LC trap column (L-column2 ODS; 0.3 × 5 mm; CERI) and a capillary column (HiQ Sil C18W-3; 0.1 × 100 mm; Techno Alpha). Digested fragments were separated for 35 min at a flow rate of 300 nL/min with a linear gradient from 2 to 100% solvent B. The solvent system consisted of 0.4 M 1,1,1,3,3,3-hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP; pH 7.0, solvent A) and 0.4 M HFIP (pH 7.0) in 50% methanol (solvent B). The eluent was ionized using an ESI source in negative mode, with a scan range of m/z 600–2000. Xcalibur 2.0.7 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for system operation.

LC-MS shotgun analyses of tRNA modification were conducted as described81 with slight modification. Five picomoles of class I tRNA fraction was digested with 50 units of RNase T1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 20 mM NH4OAc (pH 5.3) at 37°C for 45 min. Digested fragments were analyzed by a DiNa nano-flow HPLC system (Techno Alpha) coupled with an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid MS instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The percentage intensity of each modification was calculated from the ratio of mass chromatogram peak areas of RNA fragments with and without the target modification using QualBrowser in Xcalibur 4.2.28.14 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Nucleoside analyses of tRNAs were performed as described79,82. Four micrograms of total RNA were digested into nucleosides with 0.1 U of nuclease P1 (Wako Pure Chemical Industries) in 10 mM NH4OAc (pH 5.3) for 1 h at 37°C, followed sequentially by 0.1 U of phosphodiesterase I (PDase I; Worthington Biochemical Corporation) in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and 0.16 U of bacterial alkaline phosphatase (BAP; E. coli C75; Takara). For hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC)/ESI-MS, digests were dissolved in 90% acetonitrile/10% water and applied to a ZIC-cHILIC column (3 μm particle size, 2.1 × 150 mm; Merck Millipore) connected to a Q Exactive Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap MS instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and an Ultimate 3000 LC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Nucleosides were separated at a flow rate of 100 μL/min in a multistep gradient comprising 90-85% solvent B from 0 to 10 min, 85–30% solvent B from 10 to 30 min with gradient curve 7, 30% solvent B for 10 min, then a return to 90% solvent B. Proton adducts of nucleosides were scanned in positive ion mode across an m/z range of 110–950. Xcalibur 4.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for system operation.

Preparation of h2U-modified tRNAs by in vitro desulfuration
In vitro oxidation/desulfuration of s2U-modified tRNAs was conducted according to the literature56 with slight modification. Human or mouse tRNA mixtures (400 μg) were dissolved in 10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.4) and 100 mM H2O2 and incubated for 24 h at room temperature, followed by performing ethanol precipitation twice. For individual tRNAs, the isolated tRNALys (40 μg) was dissolved in 10 mM HEPES-KOH buffer (pH 7.4) and 50 mM H2O2 and incubated for 24 h at room temperature, followed by ethanol precipitation twice. For complete desulfuration, the reaction was conducted twice to achieve the highest s2U-to-h2U conversion rate.

Preparation of mRNAs for cell-free translation
The pUC-T7-HCV-HA-Rluc plasmid was used for Rluc mRNA transcription. For the control, we designed pUC-T7-HCV-mHiBiT plasmid encoding a mutant HiBiT peptide with 27 amino acids (MSTNPNTLSTTGGSSGWRLFRRISGGS) that does not contain any Lys, Glu, Gln, or Arg residues (encoded by AGR codons). For plasmid construction, a DNA segment spanning T7 promotor, HCV-IRES, and mutant HiBiT sequences was PCR-amplified from the pUC-T7-HCV-HA-Rluc plasmid as a template, followed by a second round of PCR to add an XbaI restriction enzyme site to the 3′ end of the product. The amplified product was inserted into the HindIII and XbaI sites of the same vector. Finally, according to the literature83,84, the beginning of the HCV-IRES sequence was mutated from MSTNPKPQRKT to MSTNPNTLSTT to generate the pUC-T7-HCV-mHiBiT plasmid by site-directed mutagenesis to avoid codons read by h2U-containing tRNAs. All primers used for plasmid construction are listed in Supplementary Data 6.

Plasmids were linearized by XbaI (Takara) digestion, and mRNAs were synthesized by in vitro transcription with T7 RNA polymerase using a HiScribe™ T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit (NEB).

Reconstituted human cell-free translation
Reconstituted cell-free translation was carried out as described61 with modifications. Briefly, 1.26 mg/mL eEF1 complex, 100 μg/mL eEF2, 5 μg/mL eRF1/3, 0.48 μM 40S ribosomal subunit, 0.48 μM 60S ribosomal subunit, 150 μg/mL aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase mixture, and 100 μM amino acid mixture (Promega) were mixed in a test tube in reaction buffer containing 50 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 55.2 mM potassium acetate, 6 mM magnesium acetate, 200 μM spermidine trihydrochloride, 60 μg/mL creatine kinase, 20.6 mM creatine phosphate, 1 mM DTT, 1.36 mM ATP, and 840 μM each of GTP, UTP, and CTP. This reaction mixture was then mixed with mRNA (1.56 μM Rluc mRNA, or 1.66 μM mHiBiT mRNA) and total tRNAs with or without desulfuration (1 mg/mL) in a final volume of 10 μL, followed by incubation at 32°C for 3 h.

Luciferase assay
One microliter of cell-free translation product of Rluc or mHiBiT mRNAs was used for measuring luciferase activity using a Renilla Luciferase Assay System (Promega) or a Nano-Glo HiBiT Lytic Detection System (Promega), respectively. Relative light units (RLU) of luminescence were measured by a GloMax 96 Microplate Luminometer (Promega).

Western blotting and antibodies
Cell-free translation products of Rluc mRNAs were separated by 15% SDS-PAGE and electroblotted onto an Amersham Hybond P PVDF membrane (Cytiva) using a Transblot Turbo apparatus (Bio-Rad). To detect the HA epitope of Rluc products, anti-HA-tag mAb (M180-3; MBL) was used as primary antibody at a 1:7000 dilution, and horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated donkey anti-mouse IgG (715-035-150; Jackson ImmunoResearch) was used as secondary antibody at a dilution of 1:20,000. To detect recombinant eEF-1, anti-His-tag mAb-HRP-DirecT (D291-7; MBL) was used at a dilution of 1:10,000. Target proteins were detected using Pierce ECL Plus Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Sciences) and visualized with an ImageQuant LAS4000 mini instrument (Cytiva). Band intensities were analyzed by ImageJ 1.53t.

Polysomal RNA preparation
HEK293T cells (~80% confluency) cultured in 25 dishes with 15-cm diameter were lysed with a lysis buffer comprising 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 1 mM DTT, 50 μg/mL cycloheximide. The lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C. The cell lysate was loaded onto a cushion buffer [20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 50 μg/ml cycloheximide, and 20% sucrose] and ultracentrifuged at 35,000 rpm and 4°C for 4 h by a Optima L-90K ultracentrifuge (Beckman) with a 70 Ti rotor (Beckman). Free RNA fraction was extracted from the supernatant using TriPure Isolation Reagent (Roche). The crude ribosome pellet was re-suspended in a ribosome binding buffer [20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 50 μg/ml cycloheximide], and then loaded onto a 10-50% sucrose gradient in an SDG buffer [20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 50 μg/ml cycloheximide] and ultracentrifuged at 25,000 rpm and 4°C for 4.5 h by a Optima L-90K ultracentrifuge (Beckman) with a SW28 rotor (Beckman). The gradients were fractionated with continuous measurement of absorbance at 260 nm using a TRIAX flow cell (BioComp) and a fraction collector (Gilson, Fisher Scientific). The polysomal fraction was collected, followed by RNA precipitation by adding 3 volume of ethanol and incubating overnight at –80°C85. Then, polysomal RNA was extracted from the pellet using TriPure Isolation Reagent (Roche). To concentrate small RNA fraction, polysomal RNA, free RNA, and total RNA were subjected to an anion-exchange resin (DEAE Sepharose Fast Flow; GE Healthcare) with low salt buffer [10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 250 mM NaCl, and 2 mM DTT]. After washing the resin with the same buffer, small RNA fractions were eluted with high salt buffer [10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 1 M NaCl and 2 mM DTT], followed by ethanol precipitation.

Aminoacylation assay
Aminoacylation of each tRNA was performed in a 20 μL reaction mixture containing 100 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 50 mM KCl, 6 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT, 2 mM ATP, 15–30 μM 14C-labeled amino acids, 20 μM total tRNA with or without desulfuration and 750 ng aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase mixture61 at 37°C. Before aminoacylation reaction, total tRNA was deacylated with 100 mM CHES-NaOH (pH 9.0) at 37°C for 45 min. The concentration and specific activity of 14C-labeled amino acids used in this study were as follows: 15 μM L-[14C(U)]-Threonine (6.5 GBq/mmol; American Radiolabeled Chemicals), 15 μM L-[14C(U)]-Arginine (11.1 GBq/mmol; American Radiolabeled Chemicals), 30 μM L-[14C(U)]-Glutamine (9.0 GBq/mmol; PerkinElmer), 30 μM L-[14C(U)]-Glutamic acid (8.1 GBq/mmol; American Radiolabeled Chemicals), and 15 μM L-[14C(U)]-Lysine (12.1 GBq/mmol; PerkinElmer). At each time point, the reaction was quenched by spotting 4 μL aliquots of reaction mixture onto a Whatman 3MM Chr filter paper (Cytiva). The filter paper was pre-soaked in a 5% trichloroacetic acid solution before use. The spotted filter paper was washed three times for 15 min each in ice-cold 5% trichloroacetic acid, washed with ethanol and dried under a heat lamp. Acid-insoluble radioactivity of aminoacyl-tRNAs was measured by a liquid scintillation analyzer (PerkinElmer).

Ribosomal A-site tRNA binding
tRNA binding to the A-site on the ribosome was carried out as described86,87 with modifications. mRNAs containing the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and an AAR codon (R = A or G) codons or a UUC codon (negative control) at the A-site (Supplementary Data 6) were chemically synthesized. Human cytoplasmic tRNALys bearing mcm5s2U or mcm5h2U was dephosphorylated in buffer containing 10 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5) and 0.008 units of bacterial alkaline phosphatase (E. coli C75; Takara) at 55°C for 30 min, followed by gel purification of the intact tRNAs. The dephosphorylated tRNAs were 5′ phosphorylated with [γ−32P]ATP (PerkinElmer) by T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB), followed by gel purification of the 5′−32P-labeled tRNAs. Radioactivity of labeled tRNAs was measured by Cherenkov counting using a liquid scintillation analyzer (PerkinElmer). The specific activities of labeled tRNAs were adjusted to 20,000 cpm/pmol by adding respective cold tRNALys with or without desulfuration. First, E. coli 70S ribosomes (1.6 pmol) were incubated with E. coli tRNAfMet (25 pmol) and mRNA (20 pmol) at 37°C for 40 min in binding buffer containing 50 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.5), 120 mM KCl, 6.5 mM Mg(OAc)2, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mM spermine to occupy the P-site of the ribosome. Next, 0.1, 0.25, or 0.5 pmol of the 32P-labeled tRNALys was added to the mixture and incubated at 37°C for 15 min, then at 0°C for 30 min. The mixture was spotted onto double-layered Amersham Protran nitrocellulose membrane (Cytiva) and Hybond-N+ nylon membrane (Cytiva) using a 96-well dot-blot vacuum apparatus (SANPLATEC, Japan). The membranes were washed twice with 200 μL of binding buffer, dried, exposed to an imaging plate, and visualized on an FLA-7000 image analyzer (Fujifilm). The amount of bound tRNA was quantified using Multi Gauge V3.0 (Fujifilm).

Single-particle cryo-EM analysis of ribosomes with human tRNAs
The cryo-EM single-particle analysis of the ribosome–tRNA complexes was basically performed in accordance with our previous studies5,78,86,88. E. coli 70S ribosomes were prepared from the MRE600 strain as previously described5, resuspended in RBS buffer containing 20 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 10 mM Mg(OAc)2, 30 mM NH4Cl, and 6 mM β-mercaptoethanol. Methionylation and formylation of tRNAiMet were carried out as described previously89. To form a ribosome complex, E. coli 70S ribosomes were mixed with mRNA and P-site tRNA in a mixture containing 20 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 10 mM Mg(OAc)2, 30 mM NH4Cl, 6 mM β-mercaptoethanol, 100 nM 70S ribosomes, 500 nM mRNA, and 500 nM E. coli fMet-tRNAiMet, followed by incubation at 37°C for 15 min. Next, 500 nM of human cytoplasmic tRNALys was added as A-site tRNA and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 30 min, followed by further incubation on ice for 1 h. Grid preparation was carried out as previously described5.

Ribosome particle images were collected using a Titan Krios transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV and equipped with a K3 camera (Gatan). Automated image acquisition was performed at a nominal magnification of ×105,000 with a defocus range from 0.5 to 2.5 mm using a K3 direct electron detector (Gatan) in CDS-counting mode (0.8285 Å/pixel; Supplementary Data 3). The total exposure of electrons at the specimen level was ~50 e−/Å2, and dose was fractionated into 48 frames (Supplementary Data 3).

Images were recoded as movie micrographs and image processing was performed using RELION-3.1.390. Details of image processing for each ribosome complex are described in Supplementary Fig. 5. Movies were motion-corrected with the program implemented in RELION, and contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated with CTFFIND-4.191. Ribosome particles were automatically picked by crYOLO-1.8.292. The obtained particles were initially subjected to 2D classification to discard ice contamination, and the remaining particles were then auto-refined to reconstruct a consensus map. Subsequently, based on the alignment of consensus reconstruction, 3D classification was performed. The subgroup of 70S ribosome particles was auto-refined and further classified using a mask around A-site tRNA to discard ribosomes with a vacant A-site. Subgroups of A-site tRNA-bound ribosomes were further auto-refined followed by CTF refinement, Bayesian polishing and another round of 3D refinement and postprocessing. The final resolution reached 2.26–3.18 Å. The angular distribution of particle projections was calculated by RELION-3.1.390. The local resolution of each map was estimated by RELION-3.1.390 (Supplementary Fig. 6a–d).

The high-resolution structure of the E. coli 70S ribosome complexed with P-site tRNAiMet and A-site tRNA (PDB: 7y7e)5 was used as a starting model and ridged body-fitted to the obtained cryo-EM maps. Models of mRNA and A-site tRNA were manually constructed using COOT-0.9.593, and tRNA modifications were manually inserted into the model. The chemical structure of mcm5h2U was modeled using eLBOW94. These initial models were real space-refined to cryo-EM maps by the phenix.real space refine routine95. These models were corrected using UCSF Chimera-1.1496 and COOT-0.9.593, followed by a final phenix.real space refine routine using Phenix-1.1895. Refined final models were validated using MOLPROBITY97. Map vs. model FSC values were calculated using Phenix-1.1895 (Supplementary Fig. 6e, f). Graphical figures were prepared using UCSF Chimera-1.1496 or UCSF ChimeraX 1.398.

Synonymous codon usage bias analysis
Gene lists associated with the Gene Ontology (GO) term “response to oxidative stress” (GO:0006979) were retrieved using AmiGO 2 (http://amigo.geneontology.org). Gene names were mapped to corresponding NCBI RefSeq accessions using the UniProt ID mapping tool (https://www.uniprot.org/id-mapping). The coding sequences (CDS) corresponding to the RefSeq identifiers were then downloaded from NCBI in FASTA format. For each sequence, valid open reading frames (ORFs)—defined as regions starting with a canonical ATG initiation codon and terminating at the first in-frame stop codon (TAA, TAG, or TGA)—were extracted from the FASTA files.

Relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) values were calculated using a custom Python script with Biopython v1.81, based on the observed versus expected frequencies of each synonymous codon.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In their manuscript “Translational Regulation by Desulfurated tRNA Modification: Implications for Oxidative Stress Responses” the authors identify h2U derivatives in tRNA samples prepared form several organisms and cells. The desulfurated tRNAs are described to be less efficient in the recognition of their cognate codons at ribosomes and show reduced aminoacylation efficiency.

The authors suggest that oxidative desulfuration of tRNA modulates protein synthesis under oxidative stress conditions. Nevertheless, they do not provide any evidence that those events happen in vivo and that the presence of h2U derivatives is modulated under stress conditions. The formation of these derivatives through a cellular process is indirectly demonstrated and not fully convincing, which questions the significance of the data provided regarding aminoacylation efficiency and codon-anticodon recognition.

In addition, xm5s2U modifications have been demonstrated to be important in several organisms and conditions for efficient protein translation upon stress (see for example PMID: 26052047). The formation of 2-deoxouridine derivatives can well be an unwanted damage of the tRNA, resulting in molecules that are toxic, should not participate to protein translation and are probably been degraded.

Therefore, I support the publication in Nature Communications only upon more convincing demonstration of the presence and the function of 2-deoxouridine derivatives in vivo.

In addition, I have also the following major points:
1. The oxidated form is convincingly demonstrated to be derived from mnm5s2U in bacteria, thanks to the use of E. coli ΔmnmA strain. The authors should use a similar approach in eukaryotes. Knockout of the enzymes for the 5-Methyl-2-thiouridine derivatives will strengthen the results.
2. The spike-in experiments demonstrate that h2U derivative formation during handling of tRNAs was negligible, but not that these derivatives are effectively present in the cells. These h2U derivatives could be produced, for example, during lysis when the cellular components including tRNAs get in contact with H2O2 or other cellular radicals in the mix due to the lipid membrane dissolution. I suggest to use controlled conditions in the initial lysis and also to carefully compare several lysis methods.
3. Are these h2U derivatives effectively involved in protein translation in vivo? Could these derivatives be, for example, identified and quantified in tRNAs extracted from polysomal fractions? In cells with high fractions of these derivatives ( ~15% of tRNALys in HeLa cells contained mcm5h2U), is the translation of the cognate codons effectively affected?
4. Is there is a purification step of the tRNA after H2O2 treatment? In the Methods section it is not mentioned if the left over H2O2 in the tRNA preparation was removed, as this can interfere with the subsequent reactions, for example, aminoacylation or in vitro translation.
5. The author state in the discussion „we have quantified h2U derivatives under various oxidative stress conditions, but are yet to find conditions that reproducibly increase h2U levels”. The fat that the authors did not find conditions that reproducibly increase h2U levels is a major concern to doubt the biological function of these derivatives. In any case it would be useful to show also these negative results. Which conditions and stresses have been used so far without observing any modulation?
6. In figure 4 Western of the HiBit construct is missing as control.

Minor points:
The author state “We reviewed our previous liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) data”. Please add a reference. Which previous data were reviewed?
What is the peak indicated by an asterisk in fig S1A? Please clarify in the legend.

### Reviewer 2

Review of the manuscript entitled "Translational Regulation by Desulfurated tRNA Modification: Implications for Oxidative Stress Responses" by Yufeng Mo, Kensuke Ishiguro, Kenjyo Miyauchi, Yuriko Sakaguchi, Naho Akiyama, Ayaka Murayama, Kodai Machida, Hiroaki Imataka, Akio Yamashita, Mikako Shirouzu, and Tsutomu Suzuki submitted to Nature Comminications.

The authors describe the identification of h2U derivatives in human and bacterial cells as well as in mouse liver tissue. These h2U derivatives are products of sulfur removal from natural 2-thiouridine derivatives present in four transfer RNAs specific for lysine, glutamine, glutamic acid, and asparagine. The authors claim that the h2U derivatives are the products of natural oxidative desulfuration of intact tRNAs isolated from cytoplasmic and mitochondrial fractions. In a series of mass spectrometry experiments, they confirm the presence of x5h2U at position 34 of the tRNA, which was originally the position of the xms2U derivatives. Since this is the first position of the anticodon, they examine the characteristics of the oxidized tRNA. They noted the decreased efficiency of translation in a human reconstituted in vitro system with free cells and the decreased efficiency of h2U-tRNALys, Glu and Gln aminoacylation. Finally, they concluded that desulfuration of native tRNA specific for lysine (with mcm5s2U) affects codon recognition when the damaged tRNA is bound to either a programmed AAA or AAG ribosome, by a loss of AAA codon recognition followed by to some degree decreased AAG codon recognition. To confirm the molecular structures of the mcm5h2U and A and mcm5h2U and G base pairs, they used a cryo-EM approach and discovered the “anionic type” mcm5h2U-G base pair. They also show the weak mcm5h2U-A pair (with only one hydrogen bond) as well as the two original base pairs mcms2U-A and mcm5s2U-G. In their general conclusions, they state that desulfuration of the tRNA thio-modification modulates protein synthesis under oxidative stress.

Although the data presented are convincing and to some extent original, the manuscript needs to be thoroughly revised to be considered for publication.

Major corrections:
- First of all, the presence of mcm5h2U has already been detected in yeast, several human cancer cell lines and also in modified 293 cells deprived of oxidative system gene expression and cultured under normal and oxidative stress conditions (doi: 10.3390/ijms252212336). Therefore, such statements as on page 4 and in some other fragments of the manuscript such as: “However, the occurrence of oxidative desulfuration of xm5s2U within cells has not yet been investigated.” is incorrect. The manuscript should refer to the published data and correct the text in the manuscript.
- The authors dissect the oxidative desulfuration of 2-thiouridine to a 4-pyrimidinone derivative and omit the other product, the uridine derivative. As previously reported, the composition of the products of the desulfuration reaction depends on the pH of the reaction environment and on the nature of the substituent at position 5 of the 2-thiouridine moiety (doi: 10.1016/j.bmcl.2013.08.114, doi: 10.1016/j.bmc.2015.07.030). The authors completely ignored such a xm5s2U property, did not explain how they assessed the influence of xm5h2U-tRNA and excluded the influence of the presence of xm5U-tRNA products in the investigated processes (translation/aminoacylation), which were performed under physiological conditions (pH 7.4). Of particular interest in this context is the result of binding of the oxidized mcm5S2U-tRNA to the mRNA ribosome, assuming that part of the thio-tRNA is converted to its oxo derivative, which facilitates U-A binding. Moreover, the efficiency of aminoacylation also depends on the presence of the thio modification in the wobble position (identity element for AARS). Therefore, the observed effect could be due to the presence of x5h2U and x5U-tRNA in the whole tRNA, which reduce the activity of AARS. This question needs clarification/discussion.
- The oxidative desulfuration reaction scheme shown in Figure 1b, in which only one desulfuration product xm5s2U is shown, may be misleading to the readers and is inconsistent with the previous studies conducted in vitro and in the cellular systems as discussed above. The authors are advised to correct the schematic and possibly note under the figure that only the xm5h2U type desulfuration product was monitored.
- The interpretation and discussion of the molecular structures of the base pairs of mcm5s2U/mcm5h2U with A and with G requires some clarification. The base pair mcm5s2U-A is (as expected) in a typical Watson-Crick mode, while the desulfurized base pair mcm5h2U-A has only one possible hydrogen bond. The authors claim a weak bond in this base pair. The authors can address the confirmation of their result using the previously shown data of thermodynamic measurements performed for the 4-pyrimidinone type nucleoside analogs incorporated into the RNA duplex. These data show that h2U-type units form weak base pairs with A and more stable ones with G (data are given for h2U and geranylated 2-thiouridine-containing RNA duplexes). In addition, the authors are advised to point out that in such a measurement, the addition of a silver anion (sealing properties) increases the stability of the h2U-A duplex, which is further evidence for the existence of a weak h2U-A base pair.
- Importantly, the mcms2U-G base pair is not an anionic base pair (Fig. 7c) and is incorrectly interpreted as a base pair with the hydrogen bond between N2H of G and N3H of U (hydrogen bonds marked in red). The authors should check the interpretation of the team of P. Agris, who assigned such a base pair to the C-G type, where 2-thiouridine is pre-structured to its keto-enol form and provides three hydrogen bonds between G and mcm5s2U (doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2011.12.048). Fig. 7c and the interpretation in the text should be improved.
- The sentence : “In addition, structural analyses revealed that xm5s2U34 base-pairs with the third guanosine of NNG codons at the A site of the ribosome via an anionic U • G wobble pairing 33,34” refers to only one of two different cases, in one of which the xm5s2U-G base pair can adopt “a new wobble base pair” for mnm5s2U-G (Rozow et al 2016) and in the other the C-G like mode is found for mcm5s2U-G (Vendeix et al 2012). In the following text, the description refers to the new wobble base pair mnm5s2U-G, which is not related to the discussed mcm5s2U-G case, because the electronic properties of mcm5 and mnm5 are quite different and have different effects on the dissociation of the N3H proton. This fragment of the introduction requires a more detailed comment. Ref. 34 should be placed before Ref. 33.
- Authors are advised to pay more attention to correct citation, naming of compounds and interpretation of published data: e.g. page 9: mcm5h2U-G is not an anionic base pair. Similarly, mcm5s2U-G is not an anionic base pair. Only mnm5s2U-G has been shown to form a new wobble base pair in which the ionized mnm5s2U is bound to G. The discussed h2U-G and ges2U-G form base pairs of the 4-pyrimidinone-G type, and the pair mnm5s2U-G can also be categorized in the same group of modes. The total charge of this U-unit is 0, although the charge is distributed between the nucleobase and the mnm5. Do you think that “the anionic” base pair in this case is a correct description? Please correct the text accordingly.
- It is not clear how xm5s2U prevents misdecoding of the pyrimidine ending codons NNY due to the 3’-endo sugar pucker. The topic needs reference / discussion.
- The description on page 9 is misleading: “Given that the 2-thiocarbonyl group of mcm5s2U stabilizes C3’-endo ribose puckering 31,32, mcm5s2U-G pairing should be more stable than mcm5h2U-G pairing. In addition, the 2-thiocarbonyl group of mcm5s2U promotes the acidity of the N3 atom (Ref. 37), thereby contributing to the anionic mcm5s2U-G pairing 34.” The authors provide no evidence to support the conclusion of the first statement. Also, the acidity of N3 in mcm5s2U is similar to that of the 5-non-substituted 2-thiouridine (see Ref. 37) , and the mcm5s2U-G base pairing is not anionic. Therefore, the conclusions drawn here must be properly proved and descriptions corrected.
- The discussion of the discovered/confirmed data should be deepened and completed.

Minor corrections:
- please do not introduce “2-deoxouridine” as another colloquial name for 4-pyrimidinone riboside. This name is misleading compared to usually used 2’-deoxyuridine.
- as a flag laboratory for modified nucleosides, the authors are advised to consider using a proper name for modified nucleoside, abbreviated as mcm5s2u. The proper name (used by other authors) is “5-methylcarboxymethyl-2-thiouridine” and NOT “5-methoxycarbonylmethyl-2-thiouridine”. This proper name is logical in relation to the abbreviation used: methyl – m and carboxy -c. So it is rather confusing that mcm5 is read here as “methoxy” (for which a correct abbreviation/symbol should be “mo”), “carbonyl” (it has no abbreviation, and “c” is typically used for “carboxy(l)"). The use of confusing names leads to confusion in the nomenclature of modified nucleosides.
- The references to 35 and 36, which refer to the wobble base pair U-G occurring in the major groove, are misleading. The classical pairs U-G and G-U adopt the wobble mode, but these two base pairs are NOT isosteric, the feature which is important for the ribosomal context. While the G34-U3 base pair can be accommodated on the ribosome, the U34-G3 base pair is not allowed in this spatial architecture (see the work of Westhof). “Anionic” G-U in ribosomal RNA are interesting newly discovered modes, but their discussion is not relevant here (Ref. 33).
- The description of the results – the sentence about the experiments with bacterial knock-out S2U synthetase should be corrected. You write that ”the E. coli ΔmnmA strain in which mnm5s2U is converted to mnm5U (Figure S1c)”. This is an incorrect description, as in this bacterial strain the thiolation of the nucleoside mnm5U in the tRNA is abandoned.

### Reviewer 3

This work describes the identification and mechanistic studies of a tRNA modification, mcm5h2U34, present naturally in cells and tissues. In contrast to most RNA modifications studied in the past, mcm5h2U34 seems to be derived from cellular oxidation from mcm5s2U, possibly under oxidative stress and not synthesized by a cellular enzyme. Cells contain many chemically reactive metabolic products such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) that can react non-enzymatically with RNA, however, the functional consequence of such tRNA product on translation have not been studied much. This work starts with a methodology to detect and quantify mcm5h2U34, and identification in mouse tissues. This is followed by in vitro studies of mcm5h2U34 showing its deleterious effect on translation and on tRNA charging, ending with cryo-EM structures with an atomic rationale of how mcm5h2U34 affects decoding on the ribosome. The results are of high quality and clearly presented. This exciting work provides a streamlined methodology to study the functional consequences of many potential RNA damages and provides in-depth functional analysis of this frequently occurring RNA modification.

Comment:
1. A major issue is that no cellular data is shown that accompanies the biological regulation model in Fig. 8. On p. 10, the authors state: “Indeed, we have quantified h2U derivatives under various oxidative stress conditions, but are yet to find conditions that reproducibly increase h2U levels.”? What are the conditions tested? What is the charging level of the mcm5h2U34 modified tRNAs compared to their mcm5s2U34 counterpart in cells?
2. The functional model would expect to find lower fractions of mcm5h2U34 tRNAs on the polysome compared to the total RNA input. Have the authors tested this?
3. Would mcm5h2U34 tRNA specifically affect translation of stress response proteins? This may be addressed through computational codon usage analysis.

Response to Reviewer comments:
First, we thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and helpful review of our manuscript, and for providing valuable and productive suggestions for its improvement. Our point-by-point responses to each of the reviewers’ comments are shown below. Changes to the main text are marked in yellow.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In their manuscript “Translational Regulation by Desulfurated tRNA Modification: Implications for Oxidative Stress Responses” the authors identify h2U derivatives in tRNA samples prepared form several organisms and cells. The desulfurated tRNAs are described to be less efficient in the recognition of their cognate codons at ribosomes and show reduced aminoacylation efficiency.
The authors suggest that oxidative desulfuration of tRNA modulates protein synthesis under oxidative stress conditions. Nevertheless, they do not provide any evidence that those events happen in vivo and that the presence of h2U derivatives is modulated under stress conditions. The formation of these derivatives through a cellular process is indirectly demonstrated and not fully convincing, which questions the significance of the data provided regarding aminoacylation efficiency and codon-anticodon recognition.
In addition, xm5s2U modifications have been demonstrated to be important in several organisms and conditions for efficient protein translation upon stress (see for example PMID: 26052047). The formation of 2-deoxouridine derivatives can well be an unwanted damage of the tRNA, resulting in molecules that are toxic, should not participate to protein translation and are probably been degraded.
Therefore, I support the publication in Nature Communications only upon more convincing demonstration of the presence and the function of 2-deoxouridine derivatives in vivo.
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful and constructive comments. We fully agree that demonstrating the in vivo relevance of h2U derivatives is essential to support our conclusions. In our revised manuscript, we have made several key improvements to address these important concerns.
In addition, I have also the following major points:
1. The oxidated form is convincingly demonstrated to be derived from mnm5s2U in bacteria, thanks to the use of E. coli ΔmnmA strain. The authors should use a similar approach in eukaryotes. Knockout of the enzymes for the 5-Methyl-2-thiouridine derivatives will strengthen the results.
We totally agree with reviewer #1 that knockout of the enzymes formcm5s2U in eukaryotes will strengthen the result. We have accordingly performed LC/MS analysis with yeast ctu1Δ strain in which 2-thiolation of mcm5s2U is missing. In the MS chromatograms (Figure S1d), mcm5s2U as well as mcm5h2U were absent, confirming that mcm5h2U is derived from mcm5s2U.
2. The spike-in experiments demonstrate that h2U derivative formation during handling of tRNAs was negligible, but not that these derivatives are effectively present in the cells. These h2U derivatives could be produced, for example, during lysis when the cellular components including tRNAs get in contact with H2O2 or other cellular radicals in the mix due to the lipid membrane dissolution. I suggest to use controlled conditions in the initial lysis and also to carefully compare several lysis methods.
Thank you for pointing this out. To minimize oxidation by radicals that may arise during cell lysis, we used a highly reducing conditions by adding 50 mM DTT in the initial lysis buffer. We also monitored the formation of cmnm5h2U by introducing tracer tRNA at the onset of lysis (Figure S2c). The results showed that the initial lysis conditions had little effect on the frequency of h²U derivative formation.Very recently, Prof. Sierant and Nawrot group, who first demonstrated in vitro desulfuration of s2U derivatives, reported the presence of mcm5h2U and its derivative in yeast and human cells (PMID: 39596401). Although they did not perform spike-in experiments as we did, their findings serve as an independent confirmation of the existence of h2U derivatives in cells.
3. Are these h2U derivatives effectively involved in protein translation in vivo? Could these derivatives be, for example, identified and quantified in tRNAs extracted from polysomal fractions? In cells with high fractions of these derivatives ( ~15% of tRNALys in HeLa cells contained mcm5h2U), is the translation of the cognate codons effectively affected?
Thank you for the productive suggestion. In this study, we first separated human culture cell lysate into the supernatant (free RNA) and crude ribosome fractions using a sucrose cushion (Figure 4d), followed by sucrose density gradient (SDG) centrifugation to obtain the polysome fraction (Figure 4e). Small RNAs were then obtained from the free RNA and polysomal RNA, and subjected to the LC/MS nucleoside analysis, showing that mcm5h2U is present in the polysomal RNA (Figure 4f, g). As expected, the signal intensity of mcm5h2U in the polysomal RNA was lower than that in the total RNA and free RNA fractions. These results suggest that a portion of desulfurated tRNAs participates in translation, whereas others may fail to be aminoacylated or be excluded during the codon recognition step.

We apologize for the oversight in not providing details about the steps following H O treatment. After H O treatment, the tRNA was purified by performing ethanol precipitation twice. We have now added this information to the Methods section.
5. The author state in the discussion „we have quantified h2U derivatives under various oxidative stress conditions, but are yet to find conditions that reproducibly increase h2U levels”. The fat that the authors did not find conditions that reproducibly increase h2U levels is a major concern to doubt the biological function of these derivatives. In any case it would be useful to show also these negative results. Which conditions and stresses have been used so far without observing any modulation?
Thank you for pointing this out. We have listed the negative results in Table S4. We repeatedly cultured HeLa cells under various concentrations of H O , menadione, and rotenone, and analyzed changes in mcm5h U levels. However, under none of these conditions did we observe a significant increase in mcm5h U levels. Although it remains unclear under which specific conditions h U derivatives are upregulated, desulfurated tRNAs actually have a biological function to down-regulate protein synthesis in the cell.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Review of the manuscript entitled "Translational Regulation by Desulfurated tRNA Modification: Implications for Oxidative Stress Responses" by Yufeng Mo, Kensuke Ishiguro, Kenjyo Miyauchi, Yuriko Sakaguchi, Naho Akiyama, Ayaka Murayama, Kodai Machida, Hiroaki Imataka, Akio Yamashita, Mikako Shirouzu, and Tsutomu Suzuki submitted to Nature Comminications.
The authors describe the identification of h2U derivatives in human and bacterial cells as well as in mouse liver tissue. These h2U derivatives are products of sulfur removal from natural 2-thiouridine derivatives present in four transfer RNAs specific for lysine, glutamine, glutamic acid, and asparagine. The authors claim that the h2U derivatives are the products of natural oxidative desulfuration of intact tRNAs isolated from cytoplasmic and mitochondrial fractions. In a series of mass spectrometry experiments, they confirm the presence of x5h2U at position 34 of the tRNA, which was originally the position of the xms2U derivatives. Since this is the first position of the anticodon, they examine the characteristics of the oxidized tRNA. They noted the decreased efficiency of translation in a human reconstituted in vitro system with free cells and the decreased efficiency of h2U-tRNALys, Glu and Gln aminoacylation. Finally, they concluded that desulfuration of native tRNA specific for lysine (with mcm5s2U) affects codon recognition when the damaged tRNA is bound to either a programmed AAA or AAG ribosome, by a loss of AAA codon recognition followed by to some degree decreased AAG codon recognition. To confirm the molecular structures of the mcm5h2U and A and mcm5h2U and G base pairs, they used a cryo-EM approach and discovered the “anionic type” mcm5h2U-G base pair. They also show the weak mcm5h2U-A pair (with only one hydrogen bond) as well as the two original base pairs mcms2U-A and mcm5s2U-G. In their general conclusions, they state that desulfuration of the tRNA thio-modification modulates protein synthesis under oxidative stress.
Although the data presented are convincing and to some extent original, the manuscript needs to be thoroughly revised to be considered for publication.

At the same time, we fully recognize the need for a thorough revision, as pointed out, to further improve the clarity, accuracy, and scientific rigor of the manuscript.

As previously reported, the composition of the products of the desulfuration reaction depends on the pH of the reaction environment and on the nature of the substituent at position 5 of the 2-thiouridine moiety (doi: 10.1016/j.bmcl.2013.08.114, doi: 10.1016/j.bmc.2015.07.030). Therefore, the observed effect could be due to the presence of x5h2U and x5U-tRNA in the whole tRNA, which reduce the activity of AARS. This question needs clarification/discussion.

As the reviewer rightly pointed out, previous studies have shown that oxidation of s2U derivatives can yield both 4-pyrimidinone and uridine derivatives, and that the composition of the resulting products depends on the pH of the reaction environment and the nature of the C5 substituent. Based on this finding, we have revised Figure 1b to indicate that uridine derivatives (xm5U) can also be generated by oxidation and desulfuration of xm5s2U.
Based on careful evaluation of oxidation conditions, we treated human class I tRNA fractions and isolated human tRNALys with 100 mM or 50 mM H O at pH 7.4 for 24 hours at room temperature. We confirmed that under these conditions, mcm5s2U was almost entirely converted to mcm5h2U, with only minimal formation of mcm5U (Figure S4a,b). We confirmed the reproducibility of this reaction. Thank you for this insightful comment. As correctly noted, according to Vendeix et al., 2012 (PMID: 22227389), the mcm5s2U–G base pair adopts a Watson–Crick-like geometry, and they proposed that mcm5s2U may undergo a tautmeric shift of the uracil base from keto-to-enol form, allowing it to form non-canonical hydrogen bonds with G. It is important to note, however, that there are several critical differences between the conditions used in their crystallographic analysis and those in our cryo-EM study. They solved a crystal structure of a ribosome complex with a chemically-synthesized anticodon stem-loop (ASL) and the Thermus thermophilus 30S subunit (PMID: 22227389). The crystallization was conducted under conditions involving high concentrations of precipitants and at pH 6.5. Moreover, the resolution of their electron density map was not sufficient to unambiguously determine the geometry of the base pair. In contrast, we solved a cryo-EM structure of a ribosome complex with native tRNALys purified from human culture cells and the E. coli 70S ribosome. The cryo-EM grids were prepared at pH 7.6, which is much closer to physiological conditions, compared to the crystallization conditions. As shown in Figure 7c, both the mcm5s2U34 and G3 bases are clearly visible in the cryo-EM density, which supports a wobble geometry shifted toward the minor groove.
On the other hand, structural study of E. coli tRNALys bound to Thermus thermophilus 70S ribosome performed by X-ray crystallography revealed that mnm5s2U34 forms a wobble base pair with G3 that is shifted toward the minor groove (PMID: 26791911). To enable this geometry, mnm5s2U34 must adopt a tautomeric form in which the N3 position acts as a proton acceptor; accordingly, the mnm5s2U–G3 pair has been referred to as an anionic U–G base pair (PMID: 37068913). The pKa values of N3 in various uridine derivatives have been experimentally determined (PMID: 28088758): the pKa of N3 is 9.15 for unmodified uridine, 8.05 for mcm5s2U, and 7.28 for mnm5s2U. According to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, at pH 7.6 the proportion of deprotonated N3 is approximately 2.8% for uridine, 26% for mcm5s2U, and 68% for mnm5s2U. Since these calculations assume an ideal aqueous environment, it remains unclear how these values may be affected within the ribosomal context. Nevertheless, both mcm5s2U and mnm5s2U are statistically more prone to exist in an anionic form compared to uridine. Therefore, the minor-groove-shifted geometry of the mcm5s2U34–G3 base pair observed in this study is reasonably interpreted as an anionic U–G base pair.
Notably, in the study by Vendeix et al. (PMID: 22227389), crystallization was carried out at pH 6.5, where only about 2.7% of mcm5s2U would be deprotonated at N3 according to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. This suggests that mcm5s2U was predominantly in its protonated form, which may have contributed to differences in base-pair geometry observed in their crystallographic structure.

It is well known that the signal intensity of molecules detected by mass spectrometry is significantly influenced by differences in ionization efficiency among analytes. In this study, since RNA fragments are detected as negative ions derived from their phosphate groups, we calculated the modification ratios based on the intensity ratio between each modified fragment and its corresponding unmodified counterpart in the mass chromatogram. Our previous studies have shown that differences in ionization efficiency due to base composition are minimal (PMID:29760464). 3. Structural interpretaon of the mcm5s2U-G base pair
The structural analysis and discussion related to the mcm⁵s²U-G base pair presented in Figure 7c and its corresponding Supplementary Discussion are both conceptually confusing and technically flawed. Hence, the authors' esmaon of the “ionized” state of mcm⁵s²U is both unnecessary and misleading. Unlike mnm⁵s²U, which can exist in a zwiterionic form (U), mcm⁵s²U does not ionize under physiological condions in the same way. Therefore, the concept of an “anionic base pair” is incorrect and should be avoided. As noted in Rozov et al. (Ref. 34), there is no menon of “anionic U-G wobble pairing”; this is a misrepresentaon of prior work. If needed, the more accurate terminology is “zwiter ionic U” pairing with G (see Ref. 37), though even this does not apply in the case of mcm⁵s²U.
It is actually not clear why the discussion is so extensive, since the structure of this base pairing has already been proposed and a careful comparison shows that this new cryo-TEM structure obtained by the authors is very similar, if not idencal, to the structure obtained by X-ray crystallography.
A reliable mechanisc explanaon was first provided by Vendeix et al. (2012), who described a tautomeric enol form (E4) of mcm⁵s²U that forms a C–G-like base pair via three hydrogen bonds, which is very similar to the Watson-Crick geometry. Despite possible discrepancies between their and your experimental condions, this geometry was consistently observed in both structural studies. Therefore, it is reasonable to consider this structure as the most likely conformaon under the current condions and to recognize it as such in this context.
Indeed, as shown by Vendeix et al. (2012), the enol form of mcm5s2U can form three hydrogen bonds with G3, adopting a Watson–Crick–like GC base-pairing geometry. We examined this possibility in detail. When we measured the distances between the corresponding atoms using our cryo-EM structural model (Figure IA), the values obtained for the Watson–Crick–like geometry proposed by Vendeix et al. were as follows:
• U4(OH) – G6(O): 3.8 Å
• U3(N) – G1(NH): 3.8 Å
• U2(S) – G2(NH₂): 3.6 Å
Distances in the range of 3.6–3.8 Å are too long to support hydrogen bonding interactions.
By contrast, in the geometry proposed by Rosov & Westhof, the distances are:
• U4(O) – G1(NH): 3.1 Å
• U3(N) – G2(NH₂): 2.9 Å
Therefore, based on our cryo-EM results, it is difficult to support a Watson–Crick–like geometry, and the minor groove–shifted geometry proposed by Rozov and Westhof is a more plausible interpretation (Figure IA). In addition, the resolution of the ASL + AAG codon + 30S subunit complex reported by Vendeix et al. (PDB: 3T1Y) is 2.8 Å, whereas the resolution of our native human tRNALys + AAG codon + 70S ribosome complex is 2.26 Å, indicating that our structure provides a more reliable model.
Figure IB shows the mcm5s2U–G base-pairing model from Vendeix et al. (3T1Y). In this model, a Watson–Crick–like geometry is made possible by assuming an enol tautomer of mcm5s2U, and the interatomic distances fall within 2.7–3.1 Å, which at first glance appears reasonable. However, when this structure is visualized in a CPK representation (Figure IC), three steric clashes become evident, indicating that the model is structurally strained.
Moreover, when the mcm5s2U–G pair from 3T1Y is superimposed onto our cryo-EM–derived model, a clear misalignment is observed (Figure ID). Finally, we compared the two models using the Q-score (PMID: 32042190), which evaluates the fitting between a model and the density. When the mcm5s2U–G model obtained in this study was overlaid onto the cryo-EM density and the average Q-score of the uracil base was calculated to be 0.82 (Figure IE), corresponding to a resolution of 1.28 Å. In contrast, when the 3T1Y mcm5s2U–G coordinates (Vendeix et al., 2012) were fitted into the cryo-EM density, the average Q-score of the uracil base was 0.57 (Figure IF), equivalent to a resolution of 3.17 Å. These results clearly demonstrate that our model represents a more reliable base-pairing geometry.

(2012), the ribosome complex was formed by soaking chemically synthesized ASL, mRNA, and paromomycin into crystals of the T. thermophilus 30S subunit under conditions with high concentrations of precipitants and at pH 6.5. Indeed, as the reviewer pointed out, unlike mnm5s2U, mcm5s2U does not form a zwitterion, and therefore whether it can adopt an anionic U–G base-pairing geometry is open to debate. Two first base pairs, that is N1-N36 and N2-N35 form the codon - ancodon minihelix. Modified uridines such as mcm⁵s²U at posion 34 are specifically tailored to accommodate this flexibility, enabling them to pair either with A3 (via standard Watson–Crick geometry) or G3 (via alternave, non-canonical arrangements).

Implausible Selecvity of Oxidaon Products A parcularly quesonable result reported in the manuscript is the observaon that under cellular condions, s²U undergoes only desulfuraon to yield h²U, without any formaon of the oxidized product U. This finding contradicts all earlier literature concerning the chemical behavior of 2-thiouridine under oxidave condions (e.g. Rao et al., 1974; Watanabe et al., 1980; Sochacka et al., 2011), which consistently demonstrated that U is a prominent oxidaon product of s²U, both in chemical models and in biological systems.
The absence of U in the authors' data is not explained or discussed, and given the well-documented oxidave pathways of s²U, it is difficult to accept this result without an in-depth mechanisc raonale or addional experimental validaon. As the reviewer pointed out, in our in vitro oxidation experiments using H O , the mcm5s2U derivatives in tRNA underwent desulfuration exclusively to mcm5h2U, with little formation of mcm5U. This was an unexpected result, because the previous study by Sochacka et al. (2011) reported that oxidation of s2U-containing RNA produces both h2U species and U species.
Based on that report, we had anticipated that mcm5U-containing tRNA would also be generated alongside mcm5h2U-containing tRNA, and thus assumed that the subsequent challenge would be how to separate tRNAs containing mcm5h2U from those containing mcm5U.
However, under our experimental conditions, as shown in Figure S4a,b, even after performing two rounds of oxidation, the increase in mcm5U was limited to only about 2%. In the study by Sochacka et al. (2011), chemically synthesized ASL RNA was oxidized with 100 mM H O in 10 mM Tris buffer (pH 7.4). In contrast, we oxidized human or mouse tRNA fractions with 100 mM H O in 10 mM HEPES–KOH (pH 7.4), and purified human tRNALys with 50 mM H O in the same HEPES–KOH buffer. The reason for this discrepancy is unclear, but the RNA samples themselves differ, and the different buffer composition might also contribute.
For product identification, we digested tRNA with RNase T , analyzed the resulting 12-mer RNA fragment in negative-ion mode, and quantified the species based on peak intensities in the mass chromatogram. This is a highly reliable method, and it is known that the measurement is not influenced by different chemical structures of modified nucleosides (PMID: 29760464, 27348091). Therefore, there is no doubt that mcm5s2U is converted to mcm5h2U with high yield under our conditions. Indeed, in our cryo-EM structural analysis, clear density corresponding to the mcm5h2U base was visualized.
Regarding the papers the reviewer kindly introduced, in Rao et al. (1974), tRNAs were oxidized under various conditions, but oxidation products were not analyzed. Watanabe et al. (1980) oxidized the s²T nucleoside with 116 mM H O in 50 mM sodium phosphate (pH 8.0), but because the substrate is chemically different (s2T instead of mcm5s2U), is a nucleoside rather than an RNA, and the buffer and pH conditions differ, the results are not directly comparable to ours.
